title: Frozen Berry Recall Raised to Highest Risk Level: Check Freezers for Walmart and Trader Joe's Bags

content:
The Food and Drug Administration has raised a recall of frozen organic berries sold at Walmart and Trader Joe's to Class I — its most serious category — and shoppers are being urged to check their freezers now, because the bags' best-by dates run into 2028.

On November 19, 2026, the FDA classified the recall of three frozen organic berry products as Class I, meaning the products pose a reasonable probability of serious health consequences or death. The products may be contaminated with E. coli O145:H28, a Shiga toxin-producing strain. About 154,000 bags are covered by the recall.

The three products to check are:

  • Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend, 10 oz, sold at Walmart — UPC 78742-11226; lot 6 031 01, best if used by January 31, 2028, and lot 6 041 01, best if used by February 10, 2028.
  • Great Value Organic Blueberries, 10 oz, sold at Walmart — UPC 78742-11213; lot 6 019 01, best if used by January 19, 2028; lot 6 040 01, best if used by February 9, 2028; and lot 6 163 01, best if used by June 12, 2028.
  • Trader Joe's Organic Mixed Berry Blend, 12 oz — UPC 00977654; lot 6 051 01, best before February 20, 2028.

The recalling company is Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. of San Carlos, Chile. The FDA enforcement report puts the recall at 25,549 cases. The FDA has also added the company's frozen blueberries to an import alert, meaning shipments can be held at the border.

Seventeen people in Florida and Georgia became ill, and six were hospitalized, before the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared the outbreak over on September 21. The recall itself grew in stages: it began in July with GreenWise frozen organic blueberries sold at Publix, one lot of Great Value Triple Berry Blend was added in September, and the three products above were added on October 2 after FDA investigators found company records that had not been provided earlier.

Shiga toxin-producing E. coli can cause severe stomach cramps, diarrhea that is often bloody, and vomiting, usually starting 3 to 4 days after swallowing the bacteria. Most people recover in 5 to 7 days, according to the CDC. The serious complication to know is hemolytic uremic syndrome, or HUS — a kidney condition that needs hospital care and is most likely in young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems. Anyone with a recalled bag should throw it away or return it to the store, and should not eat it.

Sources: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Nov. 19, 2026; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
